aeo.what_is: A chronic, low-grade depression lasting years, with persistent low mood and related symptoms that never fully lift.

content.temporal_criteria: Depressed mood must be present for most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years in adults (one year in children and adolescents). During this period, the person cannot be without symptoms for more than two consecutive months. Symptoms may meet criteria for major depression at times (called 'double depression'), but the baseline is chronic low-level depression.

confused_with: Major Depressive Disorder (recurrent) — MDD involves discrete depressive episodes with periods of normal mood in between, while PDD is chronic and persistent without sustained symptom-free intervals. However, someone can have both (double depression).

Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood — adjustment disorder is time-limited (usually resolves within six months after the stressor ends) and linked to a specific stressor, while PDD lasts years and is not tied to a single event.
Dysthymia vs. PDD — dysthymia is the old name for what's now called Persistent Depressive Disorder. They're the same condition, just updated terminology.
Bipolar II Disorder — if brief periods of feeling 'better' are actually hypomania (decreased sleep, increased energy, elevated mood), the diagnosis may be Bipolar II, not PDD. Careful history is key.

Personality Disorder — chronic low mood and low self-esteem can be mistaken for a personality pattern, but PDD is a mood disorder with clear depressive symptoms and responds to antidepressants and therapy.
misdiagnosis_explained.clarifying_factors: At least two years of mood tracking or retrospective history; asking about 'good months' versus 'good days'; assessing for neurovegetative symptoms (sleep, appetite, energy) beyond just sadness; ruling out hypomania; distinguishing long-standing depression from characterological pessimism.
misdiagnosis_explained.timeline_differences: MDD has discrete episodes with clear onset and remission. PDD is chronic and continuous (though it may worsen or improve slightly). Adjustment disorder resolves within months. Bipolar II has hypomanic ups; PDD does not.
misdiagnosis_explained.impairment_differences: Acute MDD episodes cause severe impairment. PDD causes chronic low-grade impairment—people often function (go to work, maintain relationships) but feel 'low' all the time and never fully well. Double depression (PDD + MDE) causes the worst impairment.

description.overview: Persistent Depressive Disorder (PDD), formerly called dysthymia, is a chronic depressive condition characterized by a depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, lasting at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children/adolescents), with additional depressive symptoms that may fluctuate in intensity. Episodes may meet criteria for major depression at times ("double depression").
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A 28-year-old describes feeling 'down' for as long as she can remember. She goes to work, sees friends occasionally, but always feels a low-level sadness, fatigue, and hopelessness. She can't remember a time when she felt genuinely happy for more than a few days.

A 40-year-old man has functioned through life—graduated college, held jobs—but he's always felt 'gray.' He has low energy, poor concentration, and a persistent sense that things won't get better. Friends describe him as pessimistic, but he's felt this way for over a decade.

A 22-year-old college student has had low mood since high school. She attends classes but underperforms, feels tired all the time, and has low self-esteem. She thought it was 'just her personality' until a therapist explained it's been depression all along.

A 35-year-old mother gets through the day but feels emotionally flat. She's been this way for years—low energy, poor appetite, trouble making decisions. Every few years, it gets worse (double depression), but even on 'good' days, she's never fully well.

A 50-year-old realizes he's been depressed most of his adult life. He's had a few severe episodes requiring treatment, but between those, he's always felt low-level sadness, low energy, and hopelessness. He thought everyone felt this way until his doctor explained PDD.

A 19-year-old has been irritable, fatigued, and pessimistic since middle school. She sleeps too much, has no motivation, and feels like 'nothing will ever be good.' Her parents thought it was typical teen moodiness, but it's persisted for over three years.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief that the chronic low mood has a name and isn't just a character flaw or weakness.
Sadness that they've lost years to depression without knowing it was treatable.
Confusion about why they feel depressed even when 'nothing bad' is happening.
Hope that treatment can bring a sense of well-being they've never experienced.
Grief about what life could have been like without chronic depression.
Validation that their suffering is real and not something they're imagining.
Fear that it's too late to change after years of living this way.

content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years (1 year in youth). B. Presence, while depressed, of at least two of: poor appetite or overeating; insomnia or hypersomnia; low energy or fatigue; low self-esteem; poor concentration or difficulty making decisions; feelings of hopelessness. C. During the period, the individual has not been without the symptoms for more than 2 months at a time. D. Criteria for a major depressive episode may be continuously present for 2 years. E. No history of manic or hypomanic episode and criteria never met for cyclothymic disorder. F. Not better explained by persistent schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia spectrum, or other psychotic disorders. G. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition. H. Causes clinically significant distress or impairment.
content.prevalence: Estimated lifetime prevalence ~2–3% in adults; somewhat higher in primary care settings. Often underrecognized due to gradual, chronic course.
content.age_of_onset: Frequently begins in adolescence or early adulthood; insidious onset is common.
content.prognosis: Chronic, fluctuating course with risk of superimposed major depressive episodes. Early detection, continuous treatment, and addressing comorbidities improve outcomes; residual symptoms are common without maintenance strategies.

circuitry: Frontolimbic network dysregulation (prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, amygdala, hippocampus) affecting sustained negative affect and cognitive control.
Default mode network hyperactivity and reduced reward network responsiveness linked to anhedonia and rumination.
neurochemistry: Altered serotonergic and noradrenergic transmission; state-dependent dopaminergic reward signaling changes.
Stress-related HPA-axis activation and inflammatory signaling may contribute to chronicity.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Polygenic risk interacts with adversity, chronic stress, sleep disruption, and medical comorbidity to maintain low-grade depressive states.

history_psychosocial: Longitudinal timeline covering at least 2 years (1 year youth), including periods of relative improvement/worsening and any superimposed major depressive episodes.
Function across school/work/relationships; sleep, appetite, energy; self-esteem and hopelessness; trauma and stressors; substance use.
Family history of mood disorders and response to prior treatments.
medical_assessment: Targeted physical/neurological exam and medication review.
Labs guided by presentation: CBC, CMP, TSH/free T4; B12/folate as indicated; screen for sleep apnea when risk is present.
standardized_measures: PHQ-9 or HAM-D for severity tracking; PHQ-2 for quick screen.
Dysthymia modules in structured interviews where available; C-SSRS for suicide risk.
risk_stratification: Assess for suicidality, self-harm, and functional deterioration; consider higher level of care for acute risk or profound impairment.
Screen for comorbid anxiety, substance use, and personality traits that complicate course.
differential_diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder (recurrent, non-chronic between episodes).
Adjustment disorder with depressed mood (time-limited, trigger-bound).
Cyclothymic disorder or bipolar spectrum (history of hypomanic symptoms).
Personality disorders (e.g., borderline) with affective instability rather than persistent baseline low mood.
evaluation.team_and_process: Collaborative care between primary care and psychiatry with psychotherapy integration; involve family/supports (with consent) for adherence and monitoring.

severity_levels.mild: Symptoms meet criteria with modest impairment; daily functioning largely intact.
severity_levels.moderate: Clear functional impact across settings; residual symptoms persist despite coping.
severity_levels.severe: Marked impairment with frequent "double depression" or prominent hopelessness.

psychological: High neuroticism, perfectionism, negative attributional style
History of trauma or chronic stress
environmental: Social isolation, low support, financial or caregiving stress

impact_on_life.school_work: Persistent low productivity, absenteeism/presenteeism, reduced advancement.
impact_on_life.social: Withdrawal, diminished motivation for activities and relationships.
impact_on_life.medical: Worse adherence to medical regimens; increased utilization.
impact_on_life.emotional: Chronic demoralization and reduced quality of life.

comorbidities: Anxiety disorders (GAD, social anxiety, panic, PTSD)
Chronic pain and somatic symptom disorders

psychotherapy: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) with behavioral activation and cognitive restructuring.
Cognitive Behavioral Analysis System of Psychotherapy (CBASP) for chronic depression, especially with interpersonal deficits.
Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) for role disputes/transitions and social support building.
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) or Mindfulness-Based CBT as adjuncts.
Couples/family work when relational patterns maintain symptoms.
medications: SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine) and SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) as first-line options.
Bupropion for low energy/anergia (avoid with seizure risk/eating disorders).
Mirtazapine for insomnia and low appetite/weight loss.
Augmentation for partial response: aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, quetiapine XR; lithium (suicide risk reduction); liothyronine (T3) in selected cases.
TCAs/MAOIs reserved for refractory cases due to side-effect and interaction profiles.
Maintenance therapy is often indicated to prevent relapse and reduce chronic symptoms.
neuromodulation: ECT for severe, psychotic, catatonic, or refractory cases (especially during "double depression").
Ketamine/esketamine under appropriate protocols for treatment-resistant depression.
lifestyle_interventions: Regular sleep–wake schedule; CBT-I for insomnia.
Structured physical activity and activity scheduling.
Nutrition supporting metabolic health; limit alcohol/cannabis.
Social rhythm stabilization and skills for problem-solving/rumination reduction.
care_coordination: Collaborative care models to sustain engagement and adherence.
Safety planning for suicidality; monitor side effects and labs when indicated (e.g., SGA metabolic profile, lithium/thyroid/renal when used).

treatment_goals: Achieve sustained symptom remission and functional recovery.
Prevent "double depression" and reduce chronic residual symptoms.
Improve self-efficacy, sleep, activity level, and social engagement.
Maintain gains with relapse prevention and continuation/maintenance treatment.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Symptoms perceived as personality or "just how I am" leading to no evaluation.
Focus on situational stress without longitudinal review showing chronicity.
Somatic presentations (fatigue, sleep issues, pain) overshadow mood assessment.
overdiagnosis_factors: Normal demoralization in response to ongoing stress misclassified without functional impairment or duration.
Adjustment disorder labeled as PDD without meeting 2-year/1-year duration and persistence criteria.
Unrecognized bipolar spectrum with subtle hypomania misread as persistent unipolar depression.

course_pattern: With pure dysthymic syndrome (no MDE in last 2 years)
With intermittent major depressive episodes, with current episode
With intermittent major depressive episodes, without current episode
features: With mood-congruent or mood-incongruent psychotic features (if criteria met during MDE)
With peripartum onset (if criteria met during MDE)
With seasonal pattern (if criteria met during MDE)

warning_signs: Worsening hopelessness or rising anergia despite routine supports.
Emergence of suicidal ideation or self-harm behaviors.
Escalation to a syndromal major depressive episode.
self_help_strategies: Daily routine with scheduled pleasant and mastery-building activities.
Consistent sleep and wake times; limit long naps.
Regular exercise and social connection goals.
Use reminders/pill organizers; track mood/sleep and share with clinician.

adolescence: Irritability and low self-esteem with academic decline; risk of substance use and social withdrawal.
adulthood: Chronic low mood impacting productivity and relationships; parenting and work-role stressors common.
older_adults: More somatic complaints, sleep disturbance, and cognitive complaints; consider medical comorbidity and drug interactions.

first_person_statements: I thought everyone felt low all the time. I didn't know there was another way to live until I got treatment.
I functioned—went to work, paid my bills—but I was never happy. It took years to realize that wasn't normal.
The hardest part was that it was chronic. It wasn't one bad episode I could recover from; it was just my baseline.
People told me to 'cheer up' or 'think positive,' but it wasn't that simple. It was like carrying a weight I couldn't put down.
When I finally tried medication and therapy, I realized what 'stable' felt like. I didn't know life could be different.
I lost my twenties to depression. I wish someone had told me sooner that it was treatable.

comparisons: It's like living under a gray cloud that never fully lifts—some days it's lighter, some days it's darker, but the sun never really breaks through.
Imagine walking through life with ankle weights on: you can still move forward, but everything feels harder and heavier than it should.
Think of it as background noise you can't turn off—a constant low hum of sadness, fatigue, and hopelessness that colors everything you do.
It's like your baseline emotional temperature is set too low, and even on your best days, you're only reaching what most people consider a bad day.

faqs.question: How is Persistent Depressive Disorder different from Major Depressive Disorder?
faqs.answer: PDD is chronic and lasts at least two years with persistent low-level symptoms. MDD involves discrete episodes of severe depression with periods of normal mood in between. You can have both at once ('double depression'), where a major depressive episode occurs on top of chronic PDD.

faqs.question: Can PDD be cured, or is it lifelong?
faqs.answer: PDD is chronic, but with treatment (antidepressants, therapy, lifestyle changes), many people achieve sustained remission and feel 'normal' for the first time. Maintenance treatment is often needed to prevent relapse.

faqs.question: Why didn't anyone tell me I had depression years ago?
faqs.answer: PDD is often underrecognized because symptoms are chronic and low-grade, so people (and even doctors) mistake it for personality or 'just how someone is.' Many people don't realize they're depressed until they experience treatment and feel better.

faqs.question: Can therapy alone treat PDD?
faqs.answer: Therapy (especially CBT, CBASP, and IPT) is very effective for PDD, but many people benefit from combining therapy with antidepressants. Chronic depression often responds best to a combination approach.

faqs.question: Will I need to take medication forever?
faqs.answer: Many people with PDD benefit from long-term or indefinite treatment to prevent relapse. After years of stability, some may attempt cautious tapers, but this should be done collaboratively with your treatment team.

faqs.question: What's 'double depression'?
faqs.answer: Double depression is when someone with chronic PDD experiences a superimposed major depressive episode. The baseline is already low, and then a severe episode makes things much worse. After the acute episode resolves, the person often returns to the chronic low mood.

faqs.question: Is PDD genetic?
faqs.answer: Yes, there's a strong genetic component. Family history of depression increases risk, though environmental factors (chronic stress, trauma, substance use) also play a role.

faqs.question: Can PDD start in childhood?
faqs.answer: Yes. PDD can begin in childhood or adolescence, where it may present as chronic irritability, low energy, and poor self-esteem. Early treatment improves long-term outcomes.

faqs.question: How do I know if my low mood is PDD or just my personality?
faqs.answer: PDD involves clear depressive symptoms (low mood, low energy, poor concentration, hopelessness, sleep/appetite changes) that cause functional impairment and meet diagnostic criteria. It's not just pessimism or a 'glass half empty' outlook—it's a treatable mood disorder.

faqs.question: Can PDD get worse over time?
faqs.answer: Yes. Without treatment, PDD often persists or worsens, with increased risk of superimposed major depressive episodes, substance use, and functional decline. Early treatment reduces these risks.

faqs.question: What if I've had PDD for decades?
faqs.answer: It's never too late to treat. Even after decades, people with PDD can experience significant improvement with the right combination of medication, therapy, and lifestyle changes. Many describe feeling 'normal' for the first time.

faqs.question: Can exercise and lifestyle changes help PDD?
faqs.answer: Yes. Regular physical activity, consistent sleep, healthy nutrition, and social connection all support mood and can enhance the effects of therapy and medication. Lifestyle changes alone are usually not sufficient for PDD, but they're an important part of treatment.

faqs.question: Is PDD less serious than Major Depressive Disorder?
faqs.answer: PDD may be less acutely severe than a major depressive episode, but its chronic nature causes significant cumulative impairment over years—lost opportunities, strained relationships, and reduced quality of life. It's a serious condition that deserves treatment.

faqs.question: Can stress cause PDD?
faqs.answer: Chronic stress, trauma, and adverse life circumstances can contribute to the development and maintenance of PDD, especially in genetically vulnerable individuals. Addressing stressors and building coping skills is an important part of treatment.

faqs.question: Will I ever feel 'happy' if I have PDD?
faqs.answer: Yes. With effective treatment, many people with PDD experience sustained improvement and report feeling genuinely happy, energized, and hopeful—often for the first time in years or even decades.

real_life_examples.person: A 19-year-old college student described feeling 'down' for at least two years with low energy, poor concentration, and low self-esteem. She rarely missed classes but consistently underperformed. Her therapist diagnosed PDD and started CBT for behavioral activation and cognitive restructuring, plus sertraline. Sleep regularization and activity scheduling improved her grades and mood. She's now in her senior year, thriving academically, and planning for graduate school.

A 42-year-old man with longstanding low mood and hopelessness experienced a superimposed major depressive episode lasting eight weeks. His psychiatrist recognized 'double depression' and started venlafaxine. CBASP therapy and activity scheduling reduced symptoms. After the acute episode resolved, he continued maintenance therapy to address the chronic PDD and has been stable for two years.

A 28-year-old woman realized she'd been depressed since her teens. She functioned—held jobs, had relationships—but always felt 'gray.' Her doctor started escitalopram and referred her for IPT. With treatment, she described feeling 'alive' for the first time, with energy, motivation, and genuine happiness. She now understands what 'normal' feels like and continues maintenance medication.

A 35-year-old mother sought help after years of chronic low mood, low energy, and hopelessness. She thought it was just her personality. Mood tracking confirmed PDD, and she started bupropion plus CBT. Within months, her energy improved, her pessimism lifted, and her family noticed she was more engaged and present. She continues therapy and medication and has had no relapses.

A 50-year-old man realized he'd been depressed most of his adult life, with a few severe episodes but always a baseline of low mood. His psychiatrist diagnosed PDD with recurrent major depressive episodes. Lithium (for relapse prevention) and ongoing psychotherapy stabilized his mood. He described finally feeling 'at peace' after decades of chronic sadness.

content.when_to_seek_help: Seek evaluation for persistent low mood or hopelessness lasting most days for several months, especially if functioning declines. Immediate help for suicidal thoughts, self-harm, psychotic symptoms, or inability to care for self.

positive_factors: Early initiation of combined psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy
Stable routines, sleep, and substance abstinence
Strong therapeutic alliance and social support
challenging_factors: Comorbid anxiety, substance use, or personality pathology
Chronic stressors, social isolation, or unemployment
Partial treatment adherence or frequent discontinuation
